recent_posts.topic_title: Ckbup: one installer for CKB command-line tools (early progress, feedback welcome)
recent_posts.author: Steven_Hert
recent_posts.content_text:
Update: ckbup can now list, switch and remove versions.
The third step is merged. You can see what’s installed, switch between versions and remove the ones you don’t need.
cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup list # every tool, its installed versions and the active one
ckbup list --available # the newest stable releases, with notes for your machine
ckbup use fnn@v0.9.1 # switch to another installed version
ckbup remove fnn@v0.10.1 # remove one you no longer need
ckbup list on my machine:
ckb v0.210.0 (active)
ckb-cli v2.0.0 (active)
ckb-debugger v1.1.1 (active)
fnn v0.10.1 (active)
ckb-light-client v0.5.4 (active)
What changed:
list shows all five tools, with installed versions newest first and the active one marked. ckbup list fnn also shows where each version lives.
list --available shows the newest 10 stable releases of each tool, and whether your machine has a build and a checksum for each. Releases without a checksum still need --allow-unverified. It uses one GitHub request per tool.
use switches versions offline. If the version isn’t installed, it prints the install command instead of downloading anything. fnn’s fnn-cli switches along with fnn.
remove won’t delete the version you’re using while other versions are installed; switch with use first. Removing a tool’s last version also takes it off your PATH.
Switching works while a tool is running. Windows won’t let a running program be overwritten, so ckbup moves the old files aside instead, and a running program doesn’t block a switch.
Installing a second version leaves the current one active, and ckbup tells you how to switch.
Tested on Windows and on Ubuntu 26.04.
Next: update, downloads that resume after a dropped connection, and an optional cache so that switching back to an older version needs no new download.
I haven’t been able to test on macOS yet. If you’re on a Mac, I’d like to hear whether use and remove work for you.

topics.title: Spark Program | CKB ClearSign: verify before you sign

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB ClearSign: verify before you sign
recent_posts.author: Raceey
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project
CKB ClearSign: a TypeScript library + CCC signer wrapper that independently verifies a transaction’s inputs and explains it in plain language before the user signs.
Repo: github.com/RaceeyXo/ckb-clearsign (MIT)
2. Applicant
RaceeyXo: software engineer (full-stack Web3, AI engineering). GitHub: RaceeyXo.
3. Problem
A CKB transaction only references its inputs by out point (txHash:index). The capacity, lock, type and data of those cells come from an indexer/RPC, and CCC trusts that answer. A lying, compromised or MITM’d RPC can make a wallet show “fee 0.0001 CKB” while the user actually signs something very different. As discussed in the October DevRel AMA, CCC deliberately trusts its indexer, and this check belongs in the wallet.
Related work: CellGuard (CKBuilder projects #48) inspects transactions against policies but resolves inputs via RPC. Pocket Node decodes transactions in-wallet. CKB Contract Flow only decodes committed transactions. ClearSign is complementary: it proves input cell data by re-hashing origin transactions and ships as a CCC signer wrapper that tools like these can sit on.
4. Solution (v0.1 already built and working)
verifyInputs: fetches each input’s origin tx, re-hashes it locally (blake2b) and rejects any mismatch. RPC-supplied cell data is never trusted.
explainTransaction: per-address CKB sent/received, xUDT movements, mint/burn, fee, and a list of type scripts it can’t explain (flagged, not guessed).
ClearSignSigner: wraps any ccc.Signer (verify → explain → user confirm → sign) and checks the signed tx hash equals the confirmed one.
Honest guarantees: two separate flags. inputDataVerified = true; chainStateVerified = false in v0.1. It explains asset movements, not contract outcomes.
5. Proof it works
Tested on Windows and Linux: 39 offline tests on 5 recorded testnet transactions (2 xUDT), plus a live public-testnet check.
Lying-RPC demo:
Plain CCC + lying RPC accepts a forged input (288 CKB reported as 10,288 CKB).
ClearSign + honest RPC: verified and explained.
ClearSign + lying RPC: blocked with ORIGIN_TX_HASH_MISMATCH before the user is asked anything.
dApp pre-fills forged cell data: blocked with PREFILLED_CELL_OUTPUT_MISMATCH.
Reproduce:
git clone github.com/RaceeyXo/ckb-clearsign
npm install
npm test
npm run demo -- --offline
(Screenshots of the demo and test runs will be added once my forum account can post images.)
6. Why a signer wrapper
A library used only by the dApp protects users from honest dApps. A malicious dApp just skips it. Real protection is in the signer/wallet, so ClearSign ships as a drop-in CCC signer wrapper, and this grant funds a pilot in a real wallet.
7. Scope & to-do (6 weeks)
Wk 1: Harden v0.1 (edge cases, cross-platform scripts, browser build), publish to npm.
Wk 2: Docs + integration guide for wallet developers.
Wk 3–4: Pilot integration in one CKB wallet (PR or fork + write-up).
Wk 5: “Trusted node” mode (verifyClient) + prototype chain-state check, documented with its limits.
Wk 6: Completion report on Nervos Talk: results, wallet feedback, next steps.
Out of scope: Spore/iCKB/DAO decoding, contract simulation.
8. Budget: $1,000
Development & testing (wks 1, 3–5): $750
Docs & integration guide (wk 2): $150
Completion report & community support (wk 6): $100
9. Milestones
M1 (wk 2): npm package v0.2 + docs
M2 (wk 4): working wallet pilot
M3 (wk 6): chain-state prototype + final report

topics.title: [DIS] KeyMe — CKB's PSBT: Open Air-Gapped Signing and the First DIY Hardware

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] KeyMe — CKB's PSBT: Open Air-Gapped Signing and the First DIY Hardware
recent_posts.author: WuodOdhis
recent_posts.content_text:
If you have used a Bitcoin hardware wallet, the flow is familiar.
A watch-only app builds a transaction. It hands it to a small device as a QR code or a file. The device shows the amount and the destination. You approve. The signed transaction goes back to the app, which broadcasts it. The machine that holds the key never talks to the internet.
Bitcoin calls that container a PSBT (Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction). The devices have names you may know: Coldcard, SeedSigner, Specter DIY. They do not share one design. They share one rule: the key lives on a device that cannot reach the network, and the device shows you what you are signing.
CKB has the same need and no open equivalent. CKB transactions are not Bitcoin transactions. They carry cells, lock and type scripts, DAO state, xUDT amounts and multisig. A Bitcoin device cannot read them. In 2020, a grant added a Ledger app for CKB; it is a closed device. There is still no open, radio-less CKB signer that a community can inspect, build and improve.
KeyMe is the CKB version. PSCT is the container, CKB’s equivalent of PSBT. KeyMe is the signer, a small, radio-less device that reads the PSCT, checks every byte, shows the transaction, and signs only after you approve. The first hardware is built on a Pico 2: a small board with a screen, a QR scanner, no radio, and no operating system. It is not a clone of a Bitcoin device; it is the shape that fits CKB.
The one-minute version
PSCT — a Partially Signed CKB Transaction — is a file with three parts: the transaction, a proof for every coin it spends, and the block headers the scripts need. The device checks that each proof hashes to the coin it claims, decodes the previous output, checks the script against its registry, and shows the amount, destination, fee and change. It signs only after you confirm. It never trusts the coordinator’s summary, an address label, or a script it does not know.
The idea is not new
In 2020, a CKB grant added a Ledger app for CKB (Nervos Talk). It proved the demand; it is a closed device.
In May 2021, Xuejie Xiao (@xxuejie), a CKB core developer, posted “RFC Draft: CKB Offline Transaction Signing Scheme” (Nervos Talk). It separated transaction assembly from signing, defined the data the signer needs, described the review step, and ended with this:
As a side project, I do plan to build a Raspberry Pi Pico powered, air gapped offline transaction signing app. With a Cortex-M0+ chip and 264 KB RAM, the Pico should be more than enough to power such an offline signing design.
It stayed a draft. The Pico build never shipped.
In September 2022, @doitian opened “CKB Open Transaction” to describe a partial CKB transaction that multiple parties can build over time (GitHub discussion). The hardware wallet is the final signer in its example:
One party works on an open transaction, changes it, and hands it to the next participant. For example, the indexer collects input cells for a user; the dApp creates the unsigned transaction based on the inputs; and the hardware wallet finally signs the transaction.
The discussion cites Bitcoin’s PSBT as prior work. The project produced an alpha demo and an RFC; the RFC was closed without merging, and the project closed in 2024. No open hardware signer shipped.
The 2021 draft planned the offline signer. The 2022 project planned the partial transaction format. Both named the hardware wallet. Neither shipped an open device. KeyMe picks up the signing half: PSCT v0 is the signed container, and the Pico 2, the current Pico, is the device.
KeyMe keeps the 2021 goal and changes what building it taught us: canonical CBOR instead of a molecule envelope; hash-bound proofs instead of full input transactions; per-script-group signatures; a registry that refuses unknown scripts; finalize-or-throw. We did not carry the draft’s Lua signing path. A signer that executes arbitrary scripts is not a signer we can verify. The 2021 draft is the ancestor; PSCT v0 is the working version.
Grant requested: $9,500, in five payments of $1,900. ETA: 3.5 months from approval. What you get: three assembled units (two for independent testers), open firmware, open hardware, and documentation.
What is already built
KeyMe’s software is not a paper design. It is the oracle the hardware will be tested against.
Layer
Status
PSCT v0
Frozen. Canonical CBOR, molecule, hash-bound input proofs, witness templates.
Verifier
42 hostile tests. Refuses unknown locks and types; never guesses.
Coordinator + signer
CLI. Builds, binds, displays, refuses, signs, finalizes.
Second implementation
Rust. Byte-identical tx_hash and full_tx_hash; 3/3 conformance vectors.
Testnet
Transfer at block 23,084,406. 2-of-3 payout at block 23,086,201.
Devnet
DAO deposit → prepare → withdraw; xUDT mint → transfer. Reproducible with the demo scripts.
Hardware
Board selected: Pico 2 (RP2350). Build starts with this grant.
The testnet transfer is 0xbb10d0b6…1a85; the 2-of-3 spend is 0x0ea1b375…535f. The DAO and xUDT runs are devnet, not public chain; the scripts are in the repository. In total: 68 tests, plus the Rust conformance run. The repository is https://github.com/WuodOdhis/keyme; the spec is spec/psct-v0.md.
What this grant delivers
Three assembled units. Two go to independent testers; one stays with the project for demos. A fourth parts set is the spare.
Firmware v0.1.0 for the RP2350: PSCT parsing, proof binding, script registry, DAO/xUDT display, secp256k1 signing, QR in/out, PIN and encrypted seed, signed boot.
A host QR page. A static page that turns a PSCT into animated QR and scans the signed frames with a phone camera. No server, no keys.
Open hardware. Carrier board, schematic, BOM, 3D-printable case.
Documentation. Build guide, flashing, test report, demo video, threat model.
Licences. MIT/Apache-2.0 for code, CERN-OHL-S-2.0 for hardware, CC-BY-4.0 for docs.
How it works
The coordinator proposes; the device verifies.
The device trusts only three things: the canonical PSCT bytes, proofs that hash to the inputs they claim, and its own account and script registry. If a lock or type is unknown, it refuses. If the CBOR is non-canonical, it refuses. If the proof, network or header is wrong, it refuses. There is no “proceed anyway” button.
The device has no operating system, no shell and no network stack. The firmware is the only code. The RP2350 boots from signed flash; the seed is BIP39, encrypted at rest with a PIN and the ATECC608B key, and decrypted only while signing. USB is power-only while signing; QR is the data path. v0.1 has no third-party audit and no lab-grade physical security; that is a v0.2 conversation.
Demo
A short concept animation shows the flow: the coordinator builds the PSCT, the frames cross the air gap, the device audits the input proofs and change lock, and a malware-swapped change output is refused. It is a simulation, not the protocol; the QR grid is illustrative, and the real verifier is the test suite. The automatic refusal is the change-output check; the destination remains a human check.
Click the still to open the interactive demo.
Normal flow
Tamper: a swapped change output is refused
Hardware
The units are off-the-shelf modules on a carrier board. No custom injection mold, no custom silicon.
Why these parts:
Pico 2 (RP2350): no radio, 520KB RAM, 150MHz, Rust, secure boot, $6. No OS, instant boot, and it is in stock.
GM65: decodes QR inside the module over UART. No camera pipeline, no DSP, no large framebuffer.
2.8-inch TFT: review screen and animated QR.
ATECC608B: stores the key that encrypts the seed at rest. It does not sign secp256k1; the RP2350 does. I am not claiming a secure enclave in v0.1.
microSD: signed firmware updates and a backup. It is not the running OS.
LiPo + charger: signing does not need a cable.
No ESP32: radio. No phone: radio and a large attack surface. No Pi SBC (Zero, 3, 4, 5): a full OS and radio. The Pico 2 is a microcontroller: no OS, no radio, instant boot.

Path to sustainability
The grant pays for the open design and the first three units; it does not fund inventory. After v0.1, the same design can be sold as an assembled, tested unit to people who do not want to source parts, print a case, or flash firmware.
DIY: the BOM and build guide stay open; anyone can build at parts cost.
Assembled: a tested reference unit with signed firmware, case, battery and a starter QR workflow, priced at the BOM plus assembly, testing and support, with a small margin.
Support: flashing, replacement parts and setup help, priced separately.
The margin from assembled units funds the next batch and the v0.2 revision: a custom PCB, a secure element and an independent audit. The design stays open; the paid product is assembly and support, not a closed lock-in. The exact price is set after the v0.1 BOM is final.
This grant is not a promise of a company or a retail product. It proves the design and the first units; the assembled path is how the work can continue without a new grant for every unit.
What this is not

No custody of mainnet funds, no mobile app, no custom injection mold, no retail packaging.

The device checks that each proof hashes to the coin it claims, decodes the previous output, checks the script against its registry, and shows the amount, destination, fee and change. It signs only after you confirm. It never trusts the coordinator’s summary, an address label, or a script it does not know.

The idea is not new

In 2020, a CKB grant added a Ledger app for CKB (Nervos Talk). It proved the demand; it is a closed device.

In May 2021, Xuejie Xiao (@xxuejie), a CKB core developer, posted “RFC Draft: CKB Offline Transaction Signing Scheme” (Nervos Talk). It separated transaction assembly from signing, defined the data the signer needs, described the review step, and ended with this:

As a side project, I do plan to build a Raspberry Pi Pico powered, air gapped offline transaction signing app. With a Cortex-M0+ chip and 264 KB RAM, the Pico should be more than enough to power such an offline signing design.

It stayed a draft. The Pico build never shipped.

In September 2022, @doitian opened “CKB Open Transaction” to describe a partial CKB transaction that multiple parties can build over time (GitHub discussion). The hardware wallet is the final signer in its example:

One party works on an open transaction, changes it, and hands it to the next participant. For example, the indexer collects input cells for a user; the dApp creates the unsigned transaction based on the inputs; and the hardware wallet finally signs the transaction.

The discussion cites Bitcoin’s PSBT as prior work. The project produced an alpha demo and an RFC; the RFC was closed without merging, and the project closed in 2024. No open hardware signer shipped.

The 2021 draft planned the offline signer. The 2022 project planned the partial transaction format. Both named the hardware wallet. Neither shipped an open device. KeyMe picks up the signing half: PSCT v0 is the signed container, and the Pico 2, the current Pico, is the device.

KeyMe keeps the 2021 goal and changes what building it taught us: canonical CBOR instead of a molecule envelope; hash-bound proofs instead of full input transactions; per-script-group signatures; a registry that refuses unknown scripts; finalize-or-throw. We did not carry the draft’s Lua signing path. A signer that executes arbitrary scripts is not a signer we can verify. The 2021 draft is the ancestor; PSCT v0 is the working version.

Grant requested: $9,500, in five payments of $1,900. ETA: 3.5 months from approval. What you get: three assembled units (two for independent testers), open firmware, open hardware, and documentation.

What is already built

KeyMe’s software is not a paper design. It is the oracle the hardware will be tested against.

Layer Status
PSCT v0 Frozen. Canonical CBOR, molecule, hash-bound input proofs, witness templates.
Verifier 42 hostile tests. Refuses unknown locks and types; never guesses.
Coordinator + signer CLI. Builds, binds, displays, refuses, signs, finalizes.
Second implementation Rust. Byte-identical tx_hash and full_tx_hash; 3/3 conformance vectors.
Testnet Transfer at block 23,084,406. 2-of-3 payout at block 23,086,201.

What this grant delivers

  • Three assembled units. Two go to independent testers; one stays with the project for demos. A fourth parts set is the spare.
  • Firmware v0.1.0 for the RP2350: PSCT parsing, proof binding, script registry, DAO/xUDT display, secp256k1 signing, QR in/out, PIN and encrypted seed, signed boot.
  • A host QR page. A static page that turns a PSCT into animated QR and scans the signed frames with a phone camera. No server, no keys.
  • Open hardware. Carrier board, schematic, BOM, 3D-printable case.
  • Documentation. Build guide, flashing, test report, demo video, threat model.
  • Licences. MIT/Apache-2.0 for code, CERN-OHL-S-2.0 for hardware, CC-BY-4.0 for docs.

How it works

The coordinator proposes; the device verifies.

The device trusts only three things: the canonical PSCT bytes, proofs that hash to the inputs they claim, and its own account and script registry. If a lock or type is unknown, it refuses. If the CBOR is non-canonical, it refuses. If the proof, network or header is wrong, it refuses. There is no “proceed anyway” button.

The device has no operating system, no shell and no network stack. The firmware is the only code. The RP2350 boots from signed flash; the seed is BIP39, encrypted at rest with a PIN and the ATECC608B key, and decrypted only while signing. USB is power-only while signing; QR is the data path. v0.1 has no third-party audit and no lab-grade physical security; that is a v0.2 conversation.

Demo

A short concept animation shows the flow: the coordinator builds the PSCT, the frames cross the air gap, the device audits the input proofs and change lock, and a malware-swapped change output is refused. It is a simulation, not the protocol; the QR grid is illustrative, and the real verifier is the test suite. The automatic refusal is the change-output check; the destination remains a human check.

Click the still to open the interactive demo.

Normal flow

Tamper: a swapped change output is refused

Hardware

The units are off-the-shelf modules on a carrier board. No custom injection mold, no custom silicon.

Why these parts:

  • Pico 2 (RP2350): no radio, 520KB RAM, 150MHz, Rust, secure boot, $6. No OS, instant boot, and it is in stock.
  • GM65: decodes QR inside the module over UART. No camera pipeline, no DSP, no large framebuffer.
  • 2.8-inch TFT: review screen and animated QR.
  • ATECC608B: stores the key that encrypts the seed at rest. It does not sign secp256k1; the RP2350 does. I am not claiming a secure enclave in v0.1.
  • microSD: signed firmware updates and a backup. It is not the running OS.
  • LiPo + charger: signing does not need a cable.

No ESP32: radio. No phone: radio and a large attack surface. No Pi SBC (Zero, 3, 4, 5): a full OS and radio. The Pico 2 is a microcontroller: no OS, no radio, instant boot.

Milestones

3.5 months, five payments of $1,900: the first at approval, then one after each milestone. Each milestone payment follows a public report and the committee’s check.

M3 10 Hostile tests; DAO and xUDT paths; firmware v0.1.0 20+ adversarial tests pass on device; signed image verified; test report

The first payment is released at approval and funds the hardware order. The kickoff report at week 1 is reviewed before the M1 payment.

If hardware costs more (tax, a part price change), I absorb it or drop the spare unit. The software is donated; the hardware is at cost. Payments are in CKB at the payment-date rate, as recent grants are.

Path to sustainability

The grant pays for the open design and the first three units; it does not fund inventory. After v0.1, the same design can be sold as an assembled, tested unit to people who do not want to source parts, print a case, or flash firmware.

  • DIY: the BOM and build guide stay open; anyone can build at parts cost.
  • Assembled: a tested reference unit with signed firmware, case, battery and a starter QR workflow, priced at the BOM plus assembly, testing and support, with a small margin.
  • Support: flashing, replacement parts and setup help, priced separately.

The margin from assembled units funds the next batch and the v0.2 revision: a custom PCB, a secure element and an independent audit. The design stays open; the paid product is assembly and support, not a closed lock-in. The exact price is set after the v0.1 BOM is final.

This grant is not a promise of a company or a retail product. It proves the design and the first units; the assembled path is how the work can continue without a new grant for every unit.

  • Not a production wallet, not certified, not an audited vault.

I am WuodOdhis. I hold a BSc in Electrical Engineering. recent_posts.content_text:
Really interesting topic and definitely an important one for Nervos.
Personally, I think the problem isn’t necessarily that people don’t care about voting. A lot of CKB holders probably don’t even know these votes are happening, or how to participate.
Maybe we should focus more on making voting easier and giving proposals more visibility. Even a simple notification when a new vote is open could make a difference.
Thanks for bringing this up, I think it’s something the community really needs to discuss more.

recent_posts.content_text:
Hi xingtian,
Thank you for the detailed review. Both points are fair, and I would rather answer them honestly than defend the draft.
On audience: I described the problem but never named who would use the result. The truth is that I have not validated demand. My assumption was that evaluation operators, benchmark researchers, and funders of AI evaluations would value a cheaper way to check a published benchmark record. That is an assumption I can test outside a grant, for example by asking a few evaluators which parts of their process most need independent verification.
On the path to the goal: The proposal implied a broader claim than the pilot can support. The defensible version is narrower and falsifiable: under stated conditions, a benchmark record’s commitments, timing eligibility, published outcomes, and scoring can be reconstructed by an independent reader from public chain data at a stated cost, with residual trust assumptions named. Milestone 1 demonstrates a reduced form of that on a native CKB network, with 16 rejection cases and a separate verifier. It does not yet show transfer to a real benchmark, and I should not have folded that into the same request.
I would rather not resubmit the same scope. If the committee is open to it, I would return with a smaller proposal built around one question: does independent verification change what an evaluation operator or funder can actually check, and at what cost? I would bring written input from at least two potential users before asking for funding, and I would report a negative result if the answer is no.
If you would prefer this to remain a community write-up rather than a funding request, I am glad to do that as well, and I would still value the committee’s view on which of the two gaps matters more.
Thanks again for the time and the specific feedback.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Will On-Chain: Tamper-Evident, Private Digital Wills on CKB
recent_posts.author: Chaichamp
recent_posts.content_text:
Applicant: Fizan (GitHub: Fizan324926)
Requested grant: $1,000 USD (equivalent in CKB at the official approval price snapshot)
Duration: 4 weeks
Disbursement: 20% (200)onapproval,80%(800) on completion and reproducible verification
License: MIT OR Apache-2.0
Making will accessible, transparent, and verifiable through CKB technology
1. Summary
Will On-Chain is an open-source testnet app for sealing, updating and releasing a digital last will, using CKB as a tamper-evident, versioned registry. The will is encrypted in the browser and the key is split among chosen guardians, so the chain, the app and the developer cannot read it. The chain holds the ciphertext (or its hash), a timestamp, a version number, and an inactivity timer that lets a named executor signal a claim if the owner stops checking in.
This is a technical MVP for a tamper-evident vault. It does not provide legal validity, and it does not claim the chain can verify a death. The scripts are unaudited and for testnet only.
2. Problem
Wills held on paper, with a lawyer, or in cloud storage can be lost, backdated, disputed or locked behind an account. Families often can’t tell whether a will exists or which version is current. Crypto holders have an extra problem: heirs may not know assets exist, and secrets can’t go into a plaintext will.
3. Why CKB
Natural versioning. Updating a will spends the old cell and creates a new one with a higher version. The chain history is the revision history.
Timelocks without keepers. CKB’s since field lets a lock script enforce “owner can act anytime, executor only after a period of inactivity” with no oracle, keeper or admin key.
Capacity returns to the owner. Storing the cell costs a refundable deposit, not a fee.
Fixed, verifiable logic. The lock script is deployed by data hash and built reproducibly, so anyone can verify and redeploy it.
Related Spark work: CRT explores general revocable timelocks and Tranfr targets fund recovery. Will On-Chain is an end-to-end document workflow (encryption, key shares, versioning, executor view) built on similar primitives.
4. How it works
Create. The owner uploads or writes a will. The browser encrypts it with AES-256-GCM and computes a SHA-256 digest.
Split the key. The key is split with Shamir secret sharing (e.g. 2-of-3) into shares exported as files or QR codes for guardians. Shares never touch the chain.
Seal. The app creates a will cell holding: version, document hash, timestamp, executor lock hash, inactivity period, and either the ciphertext or the hash plus a storage pointer for larger files.
Check in. The owner spends and recreates the cell at any time, which resets the timer. Updating works the same way with a higher version. Revoking spends the cell without recreating it.
Claim. If the inactivity period passes with no check-in, the executor can spend the cell through the timelocked path, creating a public, timestamped on-chain claim.
Release. Guardians see the on-chain claim and, per the owner’s instructions, hand their shares to the beneficiaries, who recombine them in the app to decrypt and verify the hash.
The inactivity period has no protocol default. It is set at creation by the will’s key holders, and the app simply enforces whatever they choose.
What is and isn’t private
Phase
Hidden
Visible on-chain
Sealed
Will contents, key shares
Document hash, version, timestamp, addresses, inactivity period, cell size
After a claim
Will contents (until shares are combined)
The claim and its timestamp
After release
Nothing, for those who hold enough shares
Same as above; decryption happens off-chain
Revoked
Contents stay encrypted
That a will existed and was revoked
Trust model: nothing on-chain can verify death, and the chain does not hold the decryption key. The timelock gives a public, owner-vetoable claim signal, and the guardians’ shares are the real access control. If the ciphertext is stored on-chain, it stays public forever, so its secrecy rests entirely on the encryption and the share holders.
5. Scope
In scope (testnet MVP)
A small Rust lock script (ckb-std) with two paths: owner (update, check-in, revoke) and executor (after since maturity), with tests covering premature claim, unauthorized spend, check-in resetting the timer, and stale version spend
Browser module: AES-256-GCM encryption, SHA-256 hashing, Shamir split/combine, share export/import (file and QR)
Web app using CCC with standard CKB wallets: owner dashboard (create, update, check in, revoke) and executor/beneficiary view (check maturity, claim, recombine shares, decrypt, verify hash)
Testnet deployment with tx hashes and reproducible build instructions
Short spec, threat model, privacy and legal disclaimer, demo video, feedback from 3 to 5 testers
Stretch (only if ahead of schedule): optional witness signatures over the document hash, and a hash-only mode with an IPFS pointer.
6. Timeline
Week
Work
1
Repo setup; cell data layout; lock script (owner and executor paths); ckb-testtool suite; testnet deploy
2
Browser encryption, hashing, Shamir split/combine, share export/import; create, update, check-in and revoke transactions via CCC
3
Owner dashboard and executor/beneficiary view; full create → check-in → claim → decrypt flow on testnet
4
Tester feedback and fixes; spec, threat model, disclaimer, README; demo video; final report with tx hashes
7. Budget
| Item | Amount |
|—|—|
| Lock script and tests (Week 1) | $250 |
| Crypto module and CCC transactions (Week 2) | $250 |
| Web app (Week 3) | $300 |
| Testing, docs, demo, report (Week 4) | $200 |
| **Total** | **$1,000** |
Requested in CKB at the official approval snapshot rate. No other funding has been received for this work. I’ll post a short update on this thread weekly and publish fund usage at completion.
8. Risks and limitations
Not audited. Delivery includes a self-review and a clear “unaudited, testnet only” notice. An audit is recommended before any mainnet use and is not funded here.
Key-share loss: documented in the threat model; the app warns users and supports re-splitting on update.
False or malicious claims: the owner’s check-in resets the timer, and the key holders choose the inactivity period.
Public metadata: addresses, timing and cell size are visible on-chain even while the will is encrypted. The docs describe mitigations.
Scope: if the web app runs long, the executor view takes priority over polish, and stretch items are dropped first.
9. How to verify
Public repo with the script, browser module, web app and demo, under the stated license
Reproducible script build, published code hash and deployment tx
Test suite runnable with a single documented command
Testnet tx hashes for create, check-in, update, revoke, and claim
Recorded end-to-end lifecycle, spec, threat model and deploy guide
10. Maintenance, ecosystem value and next steps
I commit to bug-fix and compatibility updates for 12 months after delivery, with a published contact for security reports. The project gives CKB a relatable, non-crypto use case and reusable pieces: a timelocked two-path lock, versioned encrypted documents, and a browser Shamir module. If the MVP works, a follow-up Community Fund DAO proposal could cover an audit, mainnet, m-of-n attestors, asset distribution and Fiber integration.

  • Browser module: AES-256-GCM encryption, SHA-256 hashing, Shamir split/combine, share export/import (file and QR)
  • Web app using CCC with standard CKB wallets: owner dashboard (create, update, check in, revoke) and executor/beneficiary view (check maturity, claim, recombine shares, decrypt, verify hash)
  • Testnet deployment with tx hashes and reproducible build instructions
  • Short spec, threat model, privacy and legal disclaimer, demo video, feedback from 3 to 5 testers

Stretch (only if ahead of schedule): optional witness signatures over the document hash, and a hash-only mode with an IPFS pointer.

6. Timeline
Week
Work
1
Repo setup; cell data layout; lock script (owner and executor paths); ckb-testtool suite; testnet deploy
2
Browser encryption, hashing, Shamir split/combine, share export/import; create, update, check-in and revoke transactions via CCC
3
Owner dashboard and executor/beneficiary view; full create → check-in → claim → decrypt flow on testnet
4
Tester feedback and fixes; spec, threat model, disclaimer, README; demo video; final report with tx hashes

7. Budget

| Item | Amount |

|—|—|

| Lock script and tests (Week 1) | $250 |

| Crypto module and CCC transactions (Week 2) | $250 |

| Web app (Week 3) | $300 |

| Testing, docs, demo, report (Week 4) | $200 |

| **Total** | **$1,000** |

Requested in CKB at the official approval snapshot rate. No other funding has been received for this work. I’ll post a short update on this thread weekly and publish fund usage at completion.

8. Risks and limitations

  • Not audited. Delivery includes a self-review and a clear “unaudited, testnet only” notice. An audit is recommended before any mainnet use and is not funded here.
  • Key-share loss: documented in the threat model; the app warns users and supports re-splitting on update.
  • False or malicious claims: the owner’s check-in resets the timer, and the key holders choose the inactivity period.
  • Public metadata: addresses, timing and cell size are visible on-chain even while the will is encrypted. The docs describe mitigations.
  • Scope: if the web app runs long, the executor view takes priority over polish, and stretch items are dropped first.

9. How to verify

  • Public repo with the script, browser module, web app and demo, under the stated license
  • Reproducible script build, published code hash and deployment tx
  • Test suite runnable with a single documented command
  • Testnet tx hashes for create, check-in, update, revoke, and claim
  • Recorded end-to-end lifecycle, spec, threat model and deploy guide

10. Maintenance, ecosystem value and next steps

I commit to bug-fix and compatibility updates for 12 months after delivery, with a published contact for security reports. The project gives CKB a relatable, non-crypto use case and reusable pieces: a timelocked two-path lock, versioned encrypted documents, and a browser Shamir module. If the MVP works, a follow-up Community Fund DAO proposal could cover an audit, mainnet, m-of-n attestors, asset distribution and Fiber integration.

Thank you, @xingtianchunyan. Signature locks and scripts that check proofs are the weak spots, and I say so there.

topics.title: [DIS] Fiber Claim Cell: Async Receive and On-Chain Claims for Fiber LSPs

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Fiber Claim Cell: Async Receive and On-Chain Claims for Fiber LSPs
recent_posts.author: Akane
recent_posts.content_text:
Following up on my earlier reply in the Fiber LSP discussion, I’m excited to share Fiber Claim Cell!
Since then, I’ve narrowed the project from a full LSP service to an on-chain claim module for existing LSPs and wallets.
The focus is receiving a Fiber payment without a usable channel, with the recipient coming online later to claim it on CKB within a defined claim window.
I’d love feedback from the Fiber team and LSP operators on how this could complement the hosted LSP work already under way.
Summary
This proposal adds an on-chain claim option for receivers with no usable Fiber channel, without the LSP taking custody of the receiver’s funds. Optional stablecoin support also covers receivers with no CKB.
The LSP funds a claim cell on CKB. Its claim path pays the designated receiver; the intended flow then uses the revealed preimage to settle the payer’s held payment.
Amount verification and claim-timing safeguards are part of the funded work. The current prototype does not yet establish that the receiver can safely claim the correct amount in every case.
Public LSPs are already under way. Fiber’s own hosted LSP support is in review. Cellula’s proposal for a public mainnet LSP, built on it, passed a Community Fund DAO vote on 16 November 2026.
Both deliver a payment over a channel the receiver already has. This work adds the path for a receiver who has none, and is meant to plug into those LSPs, not to run another one.
The mechanism already works. A draft specification, the L1 lock script, and a reference implementation of the module an LSP runs are public, and the full flow has run on three real Fiber nodes and the CKB testnet.
Receivers are meant to need no new wallet. A web page asks the wallet they already have for one signed message and does the rest itself, so that only an LSP has to switch the module on. So far this has run in a browser test with a raw key. No real wallet has been connected yet, and recovery on a second device works only for wallets whose signatures are deterministic, which leaves out passkey wallets. Which wallets work is established in package C.
The proposed core budget is USD 26,500, covering packages A, C, E and F. Packages B and D are optional; including both brings the current estimate to USD 35,500.
The final package list, auditor’s quote and CKB request will be confirmed before voting. The full set of packages is estimated to take about four and a half months.
An advance of 10% is paid on approval and counted against package A. Further payments follow acceptance; package F is reimbursed at actual cost up to its ceiling.
Where this fits
To receive a payment on Fiber, a user must be reachable and must already have a channel with enough inbound liquidity. Two efforts address this, and the second is built on the first: Cellula runs Fiber’s LSP branch plus its own fixes.
Fiber hosted LSP
Cellula public LSP
This proposal

Fiber core team: design, PR #1623
LusoCryptoLabs: DAO proposal, scale test

Model

The same model, operated as a public service
A lock script and a module that an LSP adds
Where the channel comes from
The wallet funds its side. Liquidity policy is listed as an open question
The proposal includes channels of 299 CKB for the first 1,000 wallets, funded by LusoCryptoLabs with its own capital, not the DAO grant
Not addressed. Left to the LSP

The LSP keeps the payer’s payment pending and delivers when the wallet wakes: 24 hours by default, 7 days at most, then it fails the payment back
Inherits this. Its tests state that the payee must be awake to sign
Overlaps. See below

Not addressed
Not addressed. A 299 CKB channel cannot receive more than that
Claim cell on L1

No. Funds are credited only by a channel update
No
Yes, this is the mechanism
Stablecoins, receiver with no CKB
Not designed. The only asset rule is that amount and asset match
Stablecoins not named in the proposal
Script-level support verified on testnet. The LSP fronts the cell capacity
This table is built from the documents linked in it, read on 17 November 2026. Either team may have plans that those documents do not show.
What the table shows:
The offline case is already handled. Fiber’s hosted delivery holds a payment for a sleeping wallet, which is what this project’s path A does. Path A exists in the reference implementation and is not developed further here.
An on-chain fallback is the gap this proposal targets. The public designs reviewed here do not describe an on-chain claim fallback for these cases.
These are a receiver with no channel, a payment above the receiver’s inbound capacity, and a stablecoin payment to a receiver with no CKB.
The claim cell is a natural fallback for hosted delivery. Where the hosted LSP would fail a payment back because there is no channel, no capacity, or no time left in the buffer window, it can open a claim cell instead. That is the integration proposed in package D.
What already exists
Everything below is public at Akane-CN/fiber-claim-cell and can be reproduced from the repository.
Item
Status
RFC 0001: async receive
Draft. Timing rules checked against the Fiber source at commit 21c4dfb
async-claim-lock L1 script
Implemented in Rust, 17 KB. 33 script-level tests pass in the CKB-VM verifier. The build is reproducible and checked against the deployed code hash
Lock script on testnet
Deployed. 25 on-chain checks pass for CKB and xUDT, including 15 transactions the node had to reject and did
LSP-side module
Reference implementation: registration, hold invoices, per-payment state machine, exposure cap, HTTP interface, and a refund watcher that holds no key. CKB payments only. It is a module for an LSP to run, not an LSP
End-to-end run
27 checks pass on three Fiber v0.10.1 nodes built from source, on CKB testnet
Watchtower recovery after an LSP outage
One run at real timings: recovery succeeded and 9 of 10 checks pass. The failed check concerned force-close timing; the payer still showed the payment as in flight. See Risks for the full timeline, including the brief LSP restart.
Internal review
One adversarial review each of the script and of the LSP-side and page code. Every finding and what was done about it is in review-notes.md. It is not a substitute for the audit in package E
A receive web app is also working. It turns an existing wallet into a receiver without changing the wallet: the page derives the payment secrets from one signed message, checks each claim cell against the chain, and submits the claim, which needs no signature. In a browser test on testnet, a wallet with no CKB and no Fiber node collected 248.75 CKB with no action beyond opening the page, and a second device with empty browser storage recovered the same pay link and history from the wallet alone. 11 checks pass. The test signs with a raw key; connecting a real wallet through the CCC connector is built in but has not been exercised. Recovery on another device relies on the wallet producing the same signature for the same message. Wallets that sign with passkeys do not, so for them the receiving identity lives only in the browser that created it.
The end-to-end run used an ordinary Fiber node as the payer, with no knowledge of this protocol:
Scenario
Result on testnet
Receiver wakes up and is paid over its channel
Payer paid 100 CKB, receiver got 99.9 CKB, payer got the receiver’s preimage. About 10 seconds end to end
Receiver offline, claims later on L1
A wallet that had never held CKB claimed 298.7 CKB with no signature. The LSP read the preimage from the chain and the payer’s payment then succeeded
Nobody claims
The LSP refunded after expiry. The payer’s payment failed cleanly and its channel balance returned to its original value
LSP crashes while sending a claim cell, restarts, then is down when the cell expires
The restarted LSP sent the same transaction again and only one claim cell existed. While the LSP was down, a watcher holding no key refunded the expired cell. The LSP came back, read the refund from the chain, and returned the payer’s money
Reading the Fiber source also turned up two places where the public RPC documentation disagrees with the code, and one rule it does not state. The minimum final expiry delta is 160 minutes, not the documented 16 hours. cancel_invoice works on a held payment, not only on an open invoice as documented. And a hold invoice has no hold timeout of its own, which the documentation does not say either way: the 120-second hold timeout in the code applies only to multi-part payments whose preimage is already known. The RFC is written against the code.
What this work has not yet shown:
The refund and crash scenarios shortened the claim cell’s expiry to 90 and 150 seconds. Only the watchtower run used real, hours-long timings, and it ran once. A refund at real timings has not been tested.
xUDT was verified at the script level only, not end to end.
In the watchtower path, an upstream peer that does not force-close and a preimage that reaches the watchtower late have not been run.
No real wallet has been connected to the receive page.
The receiver cannot yet check the amount it is paid against what the payer sent. See Risks.
The lock script has not been audited.
How it works
The payer pays an invoice whose hash was set by the receiver.
The LSP holds the payment and sends the receiver a wake-up push.
Path A, receiver online in time. The LSP forwards the payment with the same hash. The receiver settles, and the preimage goes to the LSP.
Path B, receiver not online or has no channel. The LSP locks the amount in a claim cell on L1. The receiver claims later, and the preimage goes on chain.
In the intended flow, the LSP uses the revealed preimage to settle upstream, completing the payer’s payment.
If the claim cell is never claimed, the LSP refunds it and cancels the invoice, and the payer gets its money back.
Both paths use a receiver-controlled payment hash. The LSP settles upstream with the revealed preimage; that preimage alone does not prove the correct amount has reached the receiver.
Safe use also depends on amount verification, confirmations and the claim cutoff described under Risks. The funded work completes and validates these checks, with client claim logic included in the audit scope.
Async receive (RFC 0001, working today). The receiver registers a pool of payment hashes with the LSP. The LSP issues hold invoices from that pool and holds an incoming payment without settling it.
Path A. The receiver wakes up and hands the LSP an invoice for the same hash. The LSP pays it over their channel, learns the preimage when the receiver settles, and settles upstream.
Path B. If the receiver does not show up, or has no channel, the LSP locks the amount in a claim cell on L1. The cell’s lock checks no signature. It only constrains outputs: a claim with the preimage can pay only the receiver, and a refund, which becomes valid at expiry, can pay only the LSP. Expiry does not close the claim path: from then until one of the two confirms, both are valid and they race. The receiver’s safety therefore also rests on client-side checks, described under Risks. The receiver claims later with a single L1 transaction and needs no CKB to do it, because the fee comes out of the cell.
Refund. If nobody claims, the LSP refunds the cell and cancels the invoice, and the payer’s payment fails with nothing lost.
Under HTLCs the payer’s payment stays pending until the receiver reveals the preimage, for at most the invoice’s final expiry delta, which Fiber caps at 14 days. This is a limit of the design, stated in the RFC.
Receiving stablecoins with zero CKB. A UDT cell needs 142 CKB of capacity that a new user does not have. On path B the LSP fronts that capacity and deducts its value from the payment at a quoted rate. The script-level version of this already passes on testnet.
Scope
The scope is the on-chain claim capability, made safe enough for an LSP operator to switch on. Everything is released under the MIT licence.
Core scope (packages A, C, E and F):
The async-claim-lock script: reproducible build, audit, mainnet deployment.
RFC 0001, revised for the timing and liveness rules found in testing.
The LSP-side module that holds a payment, opens and refunds claim cells, and settles upstream, with the safeguards an operator needs: refund watchers, an exposure cap, crash recovery.
A client library that carries the receiver’s safety checks, so wallets do not reimplement them.
Optional extensions:
B. Stablecoins: payments end to end, including capacity fronting for receivers with no CKB.
D. Hosted LSP integration: the claim path takes over where a hosted delivery cannot complete.
Dropped from the earlier draft, because others are already building them:
Holding a payment for an offline wallet that has a channel. Fiber’s hosted delivery does this, with a 24-hour default window.
A specification and implementation for giving wallets inbound channels. Fiber’s LSP support and Cellula’s LSP cover this.
A public reference LSP on mainnet. Cellula has an approved proposal for public LSP deployment and operation; channel liquidity is funded by LusoCryptoLabs, not the DAO grant.
Liquidity capital of any kind.
Work packages and budget
Engineering deliverables are fixed-price. Package E includes an estimated audit fee, which is confirmed before voting. Package F is reimbursed at actual cost up to its ceiling.
Accepted engineering packages are paid less any advance already credited to them. Delivery overruns are not added to the approved engineering prices.
The core request is currently USD 26,500 for A, C, E and F. Packages B and D are optional. The final request is set before voting from the selected packages and the confirmed audit quote.
Package
What is delivered
Budget, USD
In the core
A. Hardening
RFC 0001 revised, including a rule that lets the receiver check the amount, implemented in the module. Tests at real timings, including the point where the node returns a held payment. Before voting, two things can change the requested budget:
Audit fee. USD 10,000 of package E’s price is the auditor’s fee. It is an estimate until a firm quotes for the script and the client logic together, and the price of E moves with the quote. Any saving is returned.
Packages B and D. B depends on which stablecoin LSP operators want first. D depends on an operator agreeing to integrate and on Fiber’s LSP support being released; without both it is left out and not charged.
All packages together take about four and a half months.
Three months of maintenance after the last package are included at no extra cost.
Payment terms
Payments follow the Community Fund DAO rules. The proposed schedule is below; the applicable rules will be confirmed with the DAO stewards before voting.
Amount. The rules have budgets requested in CKB. The prices in this post are in USD. The voting post states the request as a CKB amount, converted from the final USD total at the CKB price on the day it is posted, and shows both figures.
Quorum. Three times that CKB amount, as the rules require.
Stages. The budget is over USD 10,000, so it is paid in stages. 10% of the final total is paid on approval, inside the rule’s limit of 20% and USD 10,000. That advance is not extra money: it is counted against package A, and the rest of A’s price is paid when A is accepted. Every other selected engineering package is paid in full when it is accepted. Package F is settled last, at actual cost up to its ceiling, and what is not spent is not claimed.
Final amount. The request is fixed before the voting post, from the packages finally included and the auditor’s quote, and does not change after the vote.
Reporting. At each stage, a public report of what was delivered and what was spent, as the rules require.
Disbursement. By the DAO’s funds management committee under its default rules.
Risks
Risk
How it is handled
Fiber’s LSP support or Cellula’s LSP ends up covering the same cases
The comparison under “Where this fits” is drawn from both teams’ public documents, and both are asked to correct it in this thread. Any package they already cover is dropped. The on-chain claim is built as a module they can adopt, not a competing service
Claim and refund race after expiry. The script lets a claim through after expiry until the refund confirms, so a receiver who reveals the preimage too late can lose it to a refund that lands first
The receiver’s client must stop claiming a fixed margin before expiry, and must wait for confirmations on the claim cell before revealing anything. These checks live in the client library, wallets use the library instead of reimplementing them, and the library’s claim logic is inside the audit scope alongside the script
The LSP is offline when a claim lands. The node returns the incoming payment about 161 minutes before that payment expires. An LSP that is down between a claim and that point pays the receiver and collects nothing. A payer and a receiver acting together, or one person playing both, can time a claim to an outage and take the full amount

Following up on my earlier reply in the Fiber LSP discussion, I’m excited to share Fiber Claim Cell!

Since then, I’ve narrowed the project from a full LSP service to an on-chain claim module for existing LSPs and wallets.

The focus is receiving a Fiber payment without a usable channel, with the recipient coming online later to claim it on CKB within a defined claim window.

I’d love feedback from the Fiber team and LSP operators on how this could complement the hosted LSP work already under way.

Summary

This proposal adds an on-chain claim option for receivers with no usable Fiber channel, without the LSP taking custody of the receiver’s funds. Optional stablecoin support also covers receivers with no CKB.

The LSP funds a claim cell on CKB. Its claim path pays the designated receiver; the intended flow then uses the revealed preimage to settle the payer’s held payment.

Amount verification and claim-timing safeguards are part of the funded work. The current prototype does not yet establish that the receiver can safely claim the correct amount in every case.

Public LSPs are already under way. Fiber’s own hosted LSP support is in review. Cellula’s proposal for a public mainnet LSP, built on it, passed a Community Fund DAO vote on 16 November 2026.

Both deliver a payment over a channel the receiver already has. This work adds the path for a receiver who has none, and is meant to plug into those LSPs, not to run another one.

The mechanism already works. A draft specification, the L1 lock script, and a reference implementation of the module an LSP runs are public, and the full flow has run on three real Fiber nodes and the CKB testnet.

Receivers are meant to need no new wallet. A web page asks the wallet they already have for one signed message and does the rest itself, so that only an LSP has to switch the module on. So far this has run in a browser test with a raw key. No real wallet has been connected yet, and recovery on a second device works only for wallets whose signatures are deterministic, which leaves out passkey wallets. Which wallets work is established in package C.

The proposed core budget is USD 26,500, covering packages A, C, E and F. Packages B and D are optional; including both brings the current estimate to USD 35,500.

The final package list, auditor’s quote and CKB request will be confirmed before voting. The full set of packages is estimated to take about four and a half months.

An advance of 10% is paid on approval and counted against package A. Further payments follow acceptance; package F is reimbursed at actual cost up to its ceiling.

Where this fits

To receive a payment on Fiber, a user must be reachable and must already have a channel with enough inbound liquidity. Two efforts address this, and the second is built on the first: Cellula runs Fiber’s LSP branch plus its own fixes.

Fiber hosted LSP Cellula public LSP This proposal
Who Fiber core team: design, PR #1623 LusoCryptoLabs: DAO proposal, scale test Akane-CN/fiber-claim-cell

Where the channel comes from The wallet funds its side. Liquidity policy is listed as an open question The proposal includes channels of 299 CKB for the first 1,000 wallets, funded by LusoCryptoLabs with its own capital, not the DAO grant Not addressed. Left to the LSP

What the table shows:

  • The offline case is already handled. Fiber’s hosted delivery holds a payment for a sleeping wallet, which is what this project’s path A does. Path A exists in the reference implementation and is not developed further here.

  • An on-chain fallback is the gap this proposal targets. The public designs reviewed here do not describe an on-chain claim fallback for these cases.

    These are a receiver with no channel, a payment above the receiver’s inbound capacity, and a stablecoin payment to a receiver with no CKB.

  • The claim cell is a natural fallback for hosted delivery. Where the hosted LSP would fail a payment back because there is no channel, no capacity, or no time left in the buffer window, it can open a claim cell instead. That is the integration proposed in package D.

What already exists

The minimum final expiry delta is 160 minutes, not the documented 16 hours. cancel_invoice works on a held payment, not only on an open invoice as documented. And a hold invoice has no hold timeout of its own, which the documentation does not say either way: the 120-second hold timeout in the code applies only to multi-part payments whose preimage is already known.   • No real wallet has been connected to the receive page.
  • The receiver cannot yet check the amount it is paid against what the payer sent. See Risks.
  • The lock script has not been audited.

How it works

  1. The payer pays an invoice whose hash was set by the receiver.
  2. The LSP holds the payment and sends the receiver a wake-up push.
  3. Path A, receiver online in time. The LSP forwards the payment with the same hash. The receiver settles, and the preimage goes to the LSP.
  4. Path B, receiver not online or has no channel. The LSP locks the amount in a claim cell on L1. The receiver claims later, and the preimage goes on chain.
  5. In the intended flow, the LSP uses the revealed preimage to settle upstream, completing the payer’s payment.
  6. If the claim cell is never claimed, the LSP refunds it and cancels the invoice, and the payer gets its money back.

Both paths use a receiver-controlled payment hash. The LSP settles upstream with the revealed preimage; that preimage alone does not prove the correct amount has reached the receiver.

Safe use also depends on amount verification, confirmations and the claim cutoff described under Risks. The funded work completes and validates these checks, with client claim logic included in the audit scope.

Async receive (RFC 0001, working today). The receiver registers a pool of payment hashes with the LSP. The LSP issues hold invoices from that pool and holds an incoming payment without settling it.

  • Path A. The receiver wakes up and hands the LSP an invoice for the same hash. The LSP pays it over their channel, learns the preimage when the receiver settles, and settles upstream.
  • Path B. If the receiver does not show up, or has no channel, the LSP locks the amount in a claim cell on L1. The cell’s lock checks no signature. It only constrains outputs: a claim with the preimage can pay only the receiver, and a refund, which becomes valid at expiry, can pay only the LSP. Expiry does not close the claim path: from then until one of the two confirms, both are valid and they race. The receiver’s safety therefore also rests on client-side checks, described under Risks. The receiver claims later with a single L1 transaction and needs no CKB to do it, because the fee comes out of the cell.
  • Refund. If nobody claims, the LSP refunds the cell and cancels the invoice, and the payer’s payment fails with nothing lost.

Under HTLCs the payer’s payment stays pending until the receiver reveals the preimage, for at most the invoice’s final expiry delta, which Fiber caps at 14 days. This is a limit of the design, stated in the RFC.

Receiving stablecoins with zero CKB. A UDT cell needs 142 CKB of capacity that a new user does not have. On path B the LSP fronts that capacity and deducts its value from the payment at a quoted rate. The script-level version of this already passes on testnet.

Scope

The scope is the on-chain claim capability, made safe enough for an LSP operator to switch on. Everything is released under the MIT licence.

Core scope (packages A, C, E and F):

  • The async-claim-lock script: reproducible build, audit, mainnet deployment.
  • RFC 0001, revised for the timing and liveness rules found in testing.
  • The LSP-side module that holds a payment, opens and refunds claim cells, and settles upstream, with the safeguards an operator needs: refund watchers, an exposure cap, crash recovery.
  • A client library that carries the receiver’s safety checks, so wallets do not reimplement them.

Optional extensions:

  • B. Stablecoins: payments end to end, including capacity fronting for receivers with no CKB.
  • D. Hosted LSP integration: the claim path takes over where a hosted delivery cannot complete.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal’s status is pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise your proposal.
The committee recognizes the project’s real-world value: bringing usage tracking for prepaid services into CKB in an actual retail setting is an interesting application of state primitives.

As described in the proposal, the device that updates the Cell state is controlled by the store clerk. What happens if the clerk fails to record a deduction after a customer uses the service? recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Does a commercial project have no business model, and why start it?
It has one. A coordinator fee, 0.5% on each side, taken in CKB only when a trade settles. It is not charged today. After the first year of the public hub, that fee is how the operator pays for the server and provide liquidity. Anyone who runs a hub sets their own rate, including 0%. I started it so someone can buy or sell CKB for local money without sending the coins to an exchange. The seller’s CKB stays in their own Fiber channel. The local money goes straight to the seller.
2. What does this bring to CKB?
More reason to use Fiber. Every settled trade is a hold and a payout on Fiber, for local money a swap cannot settle. If people can buy and sell CKB this way, more of them open a channel and use it. That use is what gives CKB value here. The lock is a Fiber hold invoice Fiber already ships. The code is public. Anyone can read it and host their own hub.
3. Why this amount?
The amount is the work that has to be built before this works. The solver app, so a dispute can be decided. The trading app, rebuilt for phone and desktop. The website and the store listings. The LSP, because a buyer with no channel open cannot receive. There is no open-source LSP for that yet. This grant builds one. It opens the inbound for any Fiber node, not only Fiber Studio, and stands in until that node can receive.
The CLI is not required for that. It is a terminal client, so someone can trade without the app and giving ai agent access. The app already trades without it. I will take twine-cli out of this grant and build it later when we would have had tractions, and I will update the proposal so the amount matches what is left.

CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint 项目结项报告
1. 结项评价 / Final Evaluation
结项日期 / Completion Date：2026年11月5日
1.1 评价摘要 / Evaluation Summary
CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint 是一项面向 CKB-VM 维护者的验证工具项目：以 Sail RISC-V 模型为独立参考，对固定版本解释器的指令执行逐步“对答案”，保存首个差异及可重放记录，并探索生产 Rust 代码与规范之间的机器检查证明。项目完成了严格差分工具、ADD 的条件性 Lean 4 证明、Rocq/Coq 兼容性探索，以及附带固定工具和证据的公开发布。
1.2 主要成果 / Key Achievements
交付可逐步定位差异的运行时工具。
最终公开结果覆盖 ADD 13例、ADDI 10例、BEQ 10例，共33个案例、398个提交步，双方结果全部一致；每例可单独重放。对记录轨迹注入6类差异共194次，均被识别并定位。该数字反映比较器对指定变异的检测结果，不是发现了194个 CKB-VM 漏洞。
完成与生产执行路径关联的条件性 ADD 证明。
Lean 4 定理连接生产 Rust 入口与 Sail 生成定义，覆盖 ADD 寄存器效果、x0 写入抑制和 PC 更新；另有从同一32位原始指令编码出发的解码对应定理。两者经过 kernel 检查，不依赖 sorryAx，但仍依赖明确的外部声明、工具链和状态前提。
验证对象为固定上游源码加一份受审结构补丁。补丁使动态回调字段集中于私有结构体，便于提取其余机器方法；其行为保持性接受了审查及回归测试，未得到整个程序补丁前后的形式化等价证明。
交付 Rocq/Coq 路线的可复现 NO-GO 结论。
Rust 侧遇到 result 类型命名冲突，Sail 侧遇到支持库符号缺失。项目公开阻塞点与最小复现；这一成果回答的是该固定工具组合下路线能否贯通，不计为完成 Rocq 证明。它符合提案允许以有证据的 NO-GO 完成兼容性探索的安排。
发布可恢复的源码、工具与验证证据。
week6-0.2.0 为不可变发布，包含签名、校验信息和固定工具包。项目侧报告，在全新 Ubuntu 24.04 KVM 环境中完成11阶段验证，约耗时2.5小时；CI 接收并核验证据包、重放案例。公开复现说明也记录了固定安装路径等环境要求。
1.3 创新点与价值 / Innovation & Value
项目把有限语料差分、单条指令证明和失败复现组织成可交接的维护工具，为解释器修改提供独立参考及定位线索。其生产路径提取工作也促成了 CKB-VM 上游 PR #545；截至查阅该 PR 仍为 Open，不表述为已经合并。
2. 评审过程 / Review Process
2.1 前次申请与关闭
本项目此前曾以“CKB-VM Sail Formal Verification”为名提交提案（#10214）。2026年4月29日的预审意见认可其执行层安全价值，但认为当时的大范围形式化验证计划已经超出 Spark 以低门槛、快节奏支持小型原型的范围，并要求补充可复现验收、证明边界、维护及可信依赖说明。
因此，前次申请遇到的是基础设施研究规模与 Spark 资助定位的匹配问题，并非否定这一技术方向。其程序上的关闭发生于7月8日，委员会给出的直接理由是提案停止互动超过两个月。7月31日，开发者重新申请，将长期研究收敛为维护者可使用、可检查的验证工具 MVP，才进入本轮获批范围。
2.2 重新申请与范围收敛
Tinyueng Kwan 于2026年7月31日重新申请。此前方案同时追求大范围差分及多条 Coq 证明，本次收敛为六周 MVP：强制差分覆盖 ADD、ADDI、BEQ，至少10个公开案例、5类负向测试、一条生产关联 ADD 的 Lean 4 定理，以及 Rocq/Coq 的 GO/NO-GO 报告。完整 VM 与全 ISA 验证不纳入本轮目标。
2.3 批准与执行
8月12日：委员会批准立项；8月13日确认可按计划开始。
8月14日：公布启动款交易；8月16日开发者因 JoyID 访问问题更换后续收款地址。
8月18日至27日：推进双端差分、负向测试、CI和重放流程。
9月2日：完成双侧 Lean 生成及编译，披露 Rocq NO-GO；修正 Sail 与 sail-riscv 的版本组合，并核对调整前后差分证据一致。
2.4 证明完善、延期与发布
9月10日，开发者提交 ADD 与解码对应证明，统一 Lean 工具链，并撤回此前“不需要修改生产代码”的判断。为解决动态字段提取问题，引入固定源码补丁；解码证明另依赖补丁版 Charon/Aeneas，相关信任边界公开记录。
9月15日，开发者明确尚未满足全部发布条件，并报告手臂受伤影响进度。9月23日委员会批准延期。10月10日发布 week6-0.2.0，10月13日在论坛披露交付；10月20日委员会邀请补充非技术文档，开发者于10月21日发布。
2.5 复现与最终结项
11月2日开发者询问最终验收步骤；11月3日委员会回复评审仍在进行。11月5日 Hanssen 引用 AI 复现记录，对项目达到里程碑作出肯定评价，并感谢上游 PR 的贡献。
所引复现于11月3日在隔离 Debian 13 容器中执行：Lean 检查通过；Rocq 重现预期 NO-GO；78项 Rust 测试、33例差分及194次适用轨迹变异检测通过。报告披露了补充依赖和失败重跑过程，也明确该运行不是人工审计，未采用所要求的全新 Ubuntu/KVM 环境，不构成正式签名的第三方验收提交。

本轮结论仅适用于固定版本、补丁和配置。ADDI、BEQ 只有运行时证据；ADD 为带前提的证明。全量取指与物理内存对应、平台启动可达性、MOP、cycle、ASM/JIT 等不在证明结论中。不得将本轮成果推广为完整 CKB-VM 或整条链的安全证明。
3. 资金发放详情 / Funding Details
批准预算：1,000 USD 等值 CKB。
8月12日批准公告采用1 CKB = 0.00083 USD，公布资助总额1,204,820 CKB。

4. 委员会复盘 / Spark Committee Reflection
经验1：形式化验证需要分层定义成果
源码生成、编译成功、kernel 检查和完整系统正确性是不同层次。验收应同时检查定理类型、前提、公理依赖及被证明源码身份，避免把一条带条件的指令定理扩大为整个虚拟机的保证。
经验2：复现环境与独立性应在立项时明确
干净环境发现了本地环境掩盖的缺陷；后续 AI 复现也暴露依赖与路径要求。项目侧新环境运行、CI证据重放、AI辅助执行和正式第三方签名验收，应分别说明环境、执行者及判定标准。
经验3：有证据的失败结论也是有效研究交付
Rocq 的 NO-GO 留下了可复现阻塞点，帮助后续工作减少重复探索。前提是该结果属于事先约定的可行性探索，并与必须完成的 Lean 主线分开验收。
经验4：技术可检查，也应让社区可理解
项目在受伤延期期间持续披露限制，随后补充非技术说明，将“检查什么、怎样发现差异、证据支持到哪里”解释给社区。此类说明宜成为基础设施项目的标准交付。
5. 总结 / Conclusion
CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint 将长期形式化验证方向收敛为一个可运行的工具原型，交付了三类指令的差分证据、生产关联的条件性 ADD 证明、Rocq 兼容性失败复现及可恢复发布，为后续维护与扩展建立了基础。
项目从前次超出 Spark 支持范围、后因长期未互动关闭的申请，调整为交付边界明确的验证工具 MVP，最终于2026年11月6日获委员会确认完成，结项尾款同期发放。
